Toplines US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the Russian narrative that the United States and Russia reached any kind of an agreement to end Russia’s war in Ukraine during the August 2025 Alaska Summit. Rubio stated following his meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on July 23 that Russian “proposals” at the Anchorage Summit failed and that peace will only come through new “concepts and ideas,” which Rubio stated the United States is willing to support. Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) claimed on July 23 that Lavrov reaffirmed to Rubio Russia’s readiness for negotiations and commitment to US “proposals,” to which Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at the Alaska Summit. Russian officials routinely invoke the alleged “Anchorage agreements” to advance narratives about Russia’s willingness to negotiate, despite the lack of any public statements following the summit and US officials’ recent rejections of such Russian narratives. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky continues reiterating his commitment to peace negotiations with the United States and Russia. Zelensky met with US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner on July 22 and discussed peace negotiations efforts. Zelensky reiterated on July 23 his intent to conduct trilateral US-Ukrainian-Russian negotiations sometime in Fall 2026 but noted that if the timing was up to him, these talks would occur in July 2026. Zelensky has repeatedly reiterated his commitment to peace negotiations and willingness to make meaningful compromises to end the war, despite Russian efforts to falsely paint Ukraine as the intransigent party in peace efforts. Neither Russian nor Ukrainian forces made confirmed advances on July 23. Ukrainian Operations in the Russian Federation Ukrainian forces likely continued their long-range strike campaign against Russian energy and logistics assets on July 22 and 23. Ulyanovsk Oblast Governor Alexey Russkikh claimed on July 23 that Ukrainian drones struck a fuel and energy facility in Novospassky Raion, causing a fire. Geolocated footage published on July 23 shows a fire at the NS-Oil refinery in Novospassky, Ulyanovsk Oblast (roughly 770 kilometers from the frontline). Russian opposition outlet Astra reported on July 23, citing local residents, that Ukrainian forces struck a Wildberries (the closest Russian equivalent of Amazon) warehouse near Novaya Usman, Voronezh Oblast (a suburb of Voronezh City and roughly 190 kilometers from the frontline). Geolocated point-of-view footage published on July 23 shows a fire at or near a Wildberries warehouse near Voronezh City, Voronezh Oblast. Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged a Ukrainian strike on Voronezh Oblast on July 23 but claimed that Ukrainian forces struck civilian targets. Astra reported on July 23 that Ukrainian forces struck the Subkhankulovo Linear Production and Dispatch Station in Subkhankulovo, Republic of Bashkortostan (roughly 1,200 kilometers from the frontline) on the morning of July 23 and published footage of a fire at the station. The State Committee for Emergency Situations of the Republic of Bashkortostan claimed on July 23 that debris from a Ukrainian drone caused a fire at an industrial facility in Tuymazinsky Raion, Republic of Bashkortostan. Imagery and footage published on July 23 show the crash site of a Russian forces Su-57 fighter aircraft reportedly near Lutsino, Moscow Oblast. The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that the plane crashed due to a malfunction during takeoff. Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign against Russian naval vessels and oil infrastructure has reportedly forced Russia to restrict vessel movements, petroleum product production, and shipping at Krasnodar Krai ports. Reuters reported on July 22, citing three grain industry sources, that Russia has temporarily banned the movement of naval vessels in and out of Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Krai between midnight and 0500 local time due to the Ukrainian strikes. The sources noted that authorities have only issued the order verbally, that the port is functioning normally outside of the midnight to 0500 window, and that the order has not affected grain shipments. The Kazakhstan Energy Ministry reported on July 23 that authorities have suspended loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium oil terminal at the port of Novorossiysk to ensure the safety of naval vessels and crews operating in the Black Sea, presumably referring to the threat of Ukrainian strikes against oil infrastructure and tankers. The Kazakhstan Energy Ministry reported that it is also limiting oil production to prevent overstocking oil tank farms amid restrictions on the pipeline’s oil intake volumes. Ukrainian forces escalated their long-range strike campaign that aims to isolate occupied Crimea in early July 2026, and this campaign appears to be impacting regions of Russia near Crimea, such as Krasnodar Krai. Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi reported that Ukrainian forces struck 196 Russian vessels, including oil tankers and bulk carriers, in the Black and Azov seas from July 6 to 22. Russian Supporting Effort: Northern Axis Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border Russian milbloggers claimed that Russian forces continued offensive operations in northern Sumy Oblast on July 22 and 23, but ISW does not assess that Russian forces advanced, as Ukrainian forces counterattacked. A Russian milblogger claimed on July 22 that Russian forces advanced south of Myropillya (northeast of Sumy City) and west of Kondratovka, Kursk Oblast, in an area where ISW previously assessed Ukrainian forces advanced. Russian milbloggers claimed on July 22 and 23 that Russian forces advanced south of Kindrativka, in northern Pysarivka (both north of Sumy City), and north of Myropilske (east of Sumy City). Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Velykyi Burluk direction on July 23 but did not advance. Geolocated footage published on July 23 shows Russian forces reportedly striking a Ukrainian strongpoint east of Chorne (north of Velykyi Burluk). Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Donetsk Oblast Russian objective: Capture the entirety of Donetsk Oblast, the claimed territory of Russia’s proxies in Donbas, and advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Slovyansk direction on July 22 and 23 but did not advance. Geolocated footage published on July 22 shows Russian forces striking Ukrainian positions in northern Lyman, indicating that Ukrainian forces maintain positions in the area contrary to Russian claims. A Ukrainian brigade operating in the Slovyansk direction reported on July 23 that Russian forces are concentrating experienced drone units in the brigade’s area of responsibility to strengthen Russian reconnaissance and strikes against Ukrainian positions. Russian forces conducted infiltration missions in the Kostyantynivka-Druzhkivka tactical area on a prior date. Archival footage published on June 27 and geolocated on July 22 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian positions in eastern Kostyantynivka and northeastern Novodmytrivka (just north of Kostyantynivka) after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions. The spokesperson for a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Kramatorsk direction reported on July 23 that Russian forces are avoiding direct small-arms fighting with Ukrainian forces and rely on infiltration tactics to get behind Ukrainian positions while striking Ukrainian positions with drones and artillery. The spokesperson reported that Russian forces are attempting to hide equipment in foliage while bringing it near the frontline. Russian sources continue their efforts to exaggerate Russian gains in the Kostyantynivka-Druzhkivka tactical area. Kremlin newswire TASS posted footage on June 21 of Russian forces striking Ukrainian positions in Oleksiyevo-Druzhkivka (northeast of Druzhkivka), but a geolocator identified that the footage was actually from Kostyantynivka and Kleban-Byk (south of Kostyantynivka and roughly 10 kilometers from the current frontline) and assessed that some of the footage was from around August 2025. Russian forces reportedly recently attempted a mechanized assault in the Dobropillya tactical area for the first time in over a year. A Ukrainian military source reported on July 22 that Russian forces attempted a mechanized assault from the Ocheretyne direction (in the Russian near-rear southeast of Dobropillya) with an unspecified number of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles for the first time in over a year. The source reported that Ukrainian forces repelled the assault and destroyed 80 percent of the Russian vehicles before they reached the frontline. Another Ukrainian military source implied on July 22 that Russian forces recently conducted a mechanized assault, though it is unclear if the source was referring to the attempted assault in the Dobropillya direction. ISW is unable to confirm that Russian forces conducted a recent mechanized assault in this area of the frontline. Ukrainian military units participating in combat operations typically publish footage of Russian mechanized assaults within 48 to 72 hours of the assaults, so footage supporting these preliminary Ukrainian reports may emerge in the coming days. The Russian MoD claimed on July 23 that Russian forces struck a purported Ukrainian drone control center near Dobropillya with three FAB-500 glide bombs. Geolocated footage published on July 23 shows Russian forces striking a Ukrainian command post in Dobropillya with an additional three FAB-500 glide bombs. Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Pokrovsk direction on July 22 and 23 but did not make confirmed advances. A Russian milblogger claimed on July 23 that Russian forces advanced south of Serhiivka (west of Pokrovsk). The Russian MoD claimed on July 22 that Russian forces seized Bilytske (north of Pokrovsk), but Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets reported on July 22 that Russian forces failed to advance into Bilytske and that only a few isolated Russian servicemembers are in the settlement. Russian forces are using Starlink alternatives to support communications in the Pokrovsk direction. Ukrainian 7th Rapid Reaction Corps Spokesperson Colonel Volodymyr Polevyi stated on July 23 that Russian forces are intensifying their assaults in the Pokrovsk direction using accumulated reserves and are gradually deploying the Russian-made satellite communications system Rassvet. Polevyi reported that Russian forces have deployed units from the Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies to the Pokrovsk direction and that the units are using Long Term Evolution (LTE) networks and mesh bridges to support drone activity. Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-strike campaign against Russian logistics in the Pokrovsk direction. The Ukrainian 7th Rapid Reactions Corps reported on July 23 that Ukrainian forces struck two Russian trucks near Selydove (southeast of Pokrovsk and roughly 22 kilometers from the frontline) and along the M-30 Selydove-Pokrovsk highway. The corps reported that Ukrainian forces also struck an airfield that Russian forces used to launch drones against Ukraine. Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in the Novopavlivka direction on July 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked. A Russian milblogger claimed on July 22 that Ukrainian forces are counterattacking in the Novopavlivka direction using small groups, pickup trucks, and armored vehicles. Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in the Oleksandrivka direction on July 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked. A Ukrainian brigade operating in the Oleksandrivka direction reported on July 23 that Ukrainian forces are counterattacking and striking Russian logistics in this direction. The brigade reported that Russian forces are using drones less intensely in the Oleksandrivka direction because of Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) and that Russian forces are attempting to overcome Ukrainian EW, including by frequency-hopping and using artificial intelligence (AI)-guided drones. Ukrainian forces continued mid-range strikes against Russian logistics assets in occupied Donetsk Oblast. Geolocated footage published on July 22 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian trucks along the H-15 highway near occupied Marinka (roughly 50 kilometers from the frontline). Geolocated footage published on July 21 shows a burning fuel truck in Mariupol (110 kilometers from the frontline). Russian Supporting Effort: Southern Axis Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Hulyaipole direction and in western Zaporizhia Oblast on July 22 and 23 but did not advance. Russian special services are reportedly recruiting Zaporizhzhia City residents to commit sabotage and arson. The Zaporizhia Oblast Military Administration reported on July 23 that it recorded a surge in arson attacks on administrative and civil buildings in Zaporizhzhia City. The Zaporizhia Oblast Military Administration reported that Russian special services are recruiting Zaporizhzhia City residents to commit sabotage and arson using social media and online dating sites. Geolocated footage published on July 22 shows Ukrainian forces striking a Russian military vehicle south of Myrne (roughly five kilometers from the frontline). Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Kherson direction on July 23. Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian military assets in occupied Kherson Oblast. Geolocated footage published on July 22 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian military trucks along the M-18 Melitopol-Chonhar highway near occupied Chonhar (roughly 115 kilometers from the frontline). Occupied Kherson Oblast continues to experience power outages. The Kherson Oblast occupation administration claimed on July 23 that 14 raions of occupied Kherson Oblast are without power due to an unspecified technical failure in the power grid. Ukrainian forces reportedly continued drone strikes against energy infrastructure in occupied Crimea overnight on July 22 to 23 . A local Crimea-based Telegram source claimed that there were explosions near electrical substations near occupied Feodosia, Prymorske, Haspara, Hurzuf (all about 235 to 260 kilometers from the frontline on Crimea’s southern coast), and the Balaklava Thermal Power Plant in occupied Sevastopol (about 240 kilometers from the frontline). Crimean occupation energy operator Krymenergo reported that Ukrainian strikes caused power outages and prompted energy restrictions across occupied Crimea and that the situation is most difficult in northwestern, eastern, and southern Crimea. Crimean occupation authorities claimed that Ukrainian forces targeted Crimea with drones overnight. Ukrainian forces are increasingly targeting electrical substations in occupied Crimea, including overnight on July 21 to 22. Russian Air, Missile, and Drone Campaign Russian Objective: Target Ukrainian military and civilian infrastructure in the rear and on the front line Russian forces conducted a series of drone and missile strikes against Ukraine on the night of July 22 to 23. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile and five Kh-59/69 guided missiles from occupied Crimea and 168 Shahed-type strike drones and Gerbera-, Italmas-, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Bryansk, Kursk, and Oryol cities; Primorsk-Akhtarsk, Krasnodar Krai; occupied Donetsk City; and occupied Hvardiiske, Crimea. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Ukrainian forces downed two Kh-59/69 cruise missiles and 154 drones, that seven drones struck nine locations, and that drone and missile fragments fell on four locations. Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces struck residential, fuel, electrical, and logistics infrastructure in Chernihiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Sumy, and Zaporizhia oblasts. Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces hit a private enterprise in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, killing at least four and injuring at least 27. Ukrainian Agrarian Policy Minister Taras Vysotskyi stated on July 23 that no commercial shipping vessels entered Ukrainian ports on July 22 after Ukrainian shipowners independently suspended port calls due to heightened risks of Russian strikes. Significant Activity in Belarus Russian efforts to increase its military presence in Belarus and further integrate Belarus into Russian-favorable frameworks Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko signed a decree for the Belarusian annual fall conscription cycle on July 23. Lukashenko signed a decree on July 23 to conscript Belarusian reservists into military service between September and November 2026. This activity is consistent with the usual Belarusian spring conscription cycle and is not an inflection in Belarusian military activity. Note: ISW does not receive any classified material from any source, uses only publicly available information, and draws extensively on Russian, Ukrainian, and Western reporting and social media as well as commercially available satellite imagery and other geospatial data as the basis for these reports. References to all sources used are provided in the endnotes of each update.

Toplines The Kremlin continues to reiterate Russia’s commitment to its maximalist war aims of complete Ukrainian capitulation while Russian forces fail to achieve operationally significant gains. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed on July 22 that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s June 2024 speech emphasizing Russia’s maximalist war aims, including Ukraine’s complete withdrawal from Ukrainian-controlled territory in Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts and the abandonment of Ukraine’s NATO accession aspirations before any peace negotiations, are still the basis of the Kremlin’s conditions for ending the war in Ukraine. Bloomberg reported on July 22, citing three people close to the Kremlin, that Russia is unwilling to return any Russian-occupied territories in Ukraine as part of any peace proposal and that Putin is committed to the military seizure of the remainder of Donetsk Oblast and the establishment of a “buffer zone” along the border areas of northern Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. Bloomberg noted, citing two sources close to the Kremlin, that Russia will return to peace negotiations only after seizing all of Donetsk Oblast, an objective that one source close to the Kremlin claimed that the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) has assured Putin that Russian forces can achieve by the end of 2026. Russian forces are extremely unlikely to achieve this objective before the end of 2026, however, and the Russian rate of advance in Ukraine has slowed such that ISW is not prepared to assess that Russian forces can seize all of Donetsk Oblast on any timeline. The Kremlin appears to be rejecting any territorial concessions as part of a peace proposal and is reasserting Russia’s maximalist demands, which Putin presented in 2024 at a time when Russian forces were achieving notable battlefield advances, even as Russian forces struggle to achieve meaningful territorial advances across the frontline. The Russian MoD amplified a Russian propaganda Telegram channel on July 22 claiming that Russian forces seized 2,226 square kilometers of territory in the first six months of 2026. ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces seized a net total of only 81.1 square kilometers thus far in 2026, due in part to a significant Ukrainian Spring-Summer 2026 counteroffensive and seized or infiltrated 626.85 square kilometers thus far in 2026. Russian forces do not control territory into which they have only infiltrated. Russian officials continue exaggerating Russian battlefield successes to construct a false reality that appears to be shaping Putin’s understanding of the situation and encouraging him to persist in refusing compromise on his demands. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed on July 22 that “American colleagues” have not yet rejected their “proposals” to which Russia agreed in Anchorage and that US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin reached unspecified agreements during the August 2025 Alaska Summit. Lavrov appears to have started accepting the reality that the United States and Russia did not sign any formal or legally binding agreements in Anchorage but is persisting in Kremlin claims that agreements were reached. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed on June 25 that Russia and the United States did not reach any agreement to end Russia’s war in Ukraine during the Alaska Summit. Lavrov is likely trying to set conditions to persuade the United States to officially commit to their Anchorage proposals ahead of or during his meeting with Rubio on July 23. The Kremlin appears to be setting conditions for potential mobilization and is preparing for possible civil unrest in Russia resulting from mobilization. The Russian State Duma passed a bill on July 22 that allows citizens with unexpunged and active criminal records, including for crimes related to drug smuggling and organized crime, to sign contracts with the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) during formal mobilization periods. Russian Deputy Defense Minister and Russian MoD Main Military-Political Directorate Head Army General Viktor Goremykin stated on July 22 that the July 22 bill will expand the number of Russians eligible for military service and facilitate Russian recruitment efforts for the war in Ukraine in 2026. Russia’s militarized internal security force, Rosgvardia, published proposed amendments on July 21 to expand its civil defense regulations to protect Russian society from unspecified “dangers” during mobilization, martial law, and in wartime. Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a bill in November 2025 that allows him to deploy reservists to combat areas without declaring mobilization, and ISW assessed at the time that the Kremlin would likely leverage this bill to conduct rolling partial reserve call-ups. The Kremlin appears to be setting conditions to announce formal mobilization and potentially declare martial law in Russia in anticipation of civil unrest as mobilization remains highly unpopular within Russian society. Mobilization remains a very personal decision for Putin and is ultimately contingent on Putin’s personal perception of the battlefield situation and the Kremlin’s stability, and it remains unclear whether Putin will make such a decision in the near future or what his mobilization announcement would look like. Russian President Vladimir Putin is attempting to downplay Russia’s economic problems despite the ongoing fuel shortage crisis and broader Russian economic decline. Putin held a meeting on July 22 on the current Russia’s economic situation and claimed that Russia’s economy is stable despite “external attempts to destabilize the fuel and energy sector,” referring to Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign against Russian energy infrastructure. Putin dismissed Russian fuel market issues as temporary and claimed that they will not affect Russia’s economic dynamics. Putin claimed that Russian Ministry of Economic Development data indicates that Russia’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 0.3 percent in May 2026 and by 0.2 percent in the first five months of 2026. Putin claimed that the Russian government ran a 196-billion-ruble (about $2.51 billion) surplus in June 2026 and that the Russian money supply grew by 13 percent year on year as of July 1, 2026. Putin’s July 22 statements follow a recent string of Russian officials attempting to portray Russia’s economy as stable despite the ongoing fuel shortages and other economic issues. Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Alexander Novak and Russian State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin both claimed on July 21 that Russian economic policies are stabilizing the fuel market, and Zaporizhia Oblast occupation governor Yevgeny Balitsky claimed on July 20 during a meeting with Putin that Russian authorities secured energy facilities in occupied Zaporizhia against Ukrainian drone strikes. Putin himself admitted during the July 22 meeting that Russia’s economy has shown “modest” GDP growth, and the data Putin presented suggests that Russia’s economy will likely continue struggling with inflation as the money supply increases. Russian food supplier and manufacturer association Rusprodsoyuz told Kremlin newswire TASS on July 21 that the cost of Russia’s monthly minimum food basket grew by 7.9 percent since the start of 2026, signaling that Russia’s economy is struggling with inflation. ISW has observed a number of indicators of Russia’s economic decline, including the fact that the Moscow Exchange Composite Stock Index (IMOEX) on July 16 experienced the largest single-day decline since September 2022, Russia’s reduction of agricultural exports amidst Ukrainian strikes against energy infrastructure and vessels in the Azov and Black seas, and reports of Russian capital flight. Russian business newspaper Kommersant reported on July 20, citing a report by analytics agency Platts, that Russian refineries have yet to fulfill over 81 percent of the gasoline purchase requests despite some oil refineries resuming fuel sales. Russian authorities continue to struggle to mitigate fuel shortages and energy disruptions in Russia and occupied Ukraine including in occupied Crimea, with little indication that these shortages are temporary as Putin and other Russian officials claim. ISW continues to assess that the Russian government has adopted suboptimal economic policies to sustain its war in Ukraine, leading to many of Russia’s current economic issues, including increased and unsustainable war spending, growing inflation, significant labor shortages within the construction and services industries, and reductions in Russia’s sovereign wealth fund. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Ukrainian General Staff Deputy Chief Major General Ihor Skybyuk as the chief of the Ukrainian General Staff on July 22 to replace Major General Andriy Hnatov. Skybyuk has served as the deputy chief of the Ukrainian General Staff since June 3, 2025 and was the Ukrainian Airborne Assault Forces commander from February 11, 2024 to June 3, 2025. Ukrainian Operations in the Russian Federation Ukrainian forces struck oil infrastructure and Wildberries (the closest Russian equivalent of Amazon) warehouses in Krasnodar and Stavropol krais overnight on July 21 to 22. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported on July 22 that Ukrainian forces struck logistics centers involved in providing Russian forces with drone components and navigation equipment and an oil depot in Krasnodar Krai and Stavropol Krai. Krasnodar Krai authorities acknowledged on July 21 that over 16 Ukrainian drones targeted Armavir, Krasnodar Krai (about 475 kilometers from the frontline) and that an unspecified number struck an oil depot, causing a large fire. Geolocated footage published on July 21 shows fires burning at Wildberries logistics hubs in Krasnodar City (roughly 360 kilometers from the frontline) and Nevinnomyssk, Stavropol Krai (roughly 550 kilometers from the frontline). Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim acknowledged on July 21 that Ukrainian forces struck two Wildberries logistics centers in Krasnodar City and Nevinnomyssk. Ukrainian forces previously struck several Wildberries warehouses in Moscow Oblast and Tambov Oblast on the nights of July 18 to 19 and 20 to 21. Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign continues to force Russian authorities to restrict airspace in Moscow City. Russian outlet Kommersant reported on July 22 that Russian state aviation regulator Rosaviatsia issued a notice to airmen (NOTAM) lowering flight altitudes near Moscow City to 4,900 meters and banned transit flights over the city. Kommersant noted that the ban on transit flights will reduce the volume of flights but increase fuel consumption and flight time. Rosaviatsia previously restricted civilian flight altitudes to 5,200 in the airspace above Moscow City, most of Moscow Oblast, and parts of Ryazan, Tula, Kaluga, Tver, Yaroslavl, and Vladimir oblasts on June 17, 2026, but Ukrainian strikes against Russian territory have only intensified since then. ISW continues to assess that Russia has largely failed to defend its rear against Ukrainian strikes and that growing airspace restrictions are part of the Kremlin’s effort to mitigate the threat of Ukrainian drones. A Russian milblogger claimed on July 21 that Ukrainian forces counterattacked near Yunakivka (northeast of Sumy City). Geolocated footage published on July 22 shows Ukrainian forces striking a Russian fuel and lubricants depot in Brovnichi, Bryansk Oblast (on the international border with Chernihiv Oblast). The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed on July 22 that elements of the Russian 34th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade (49th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Southern Military District [SMD]) and of the 11th Tank Regiment (18th Motorized Rifle Division, 11th Army Corps [AC], Leningrad Military District [LMD]) seized Artilne (northeast of Velykyi Burluk). A Russian milblogger claimed on July 22 that Russian forces seized Hrafske (northeast of Kharkiv City). Russian sources continue to post likely artificial intelligence (AI)-altered footage of flag-raising events as part of a cognitive warfare effort aimed at exaggerating Russian advances. Geolocated footage published on July 20 shows Russian forces raising flags in Hrafske (northeast of Kharkiv City). ISW has reason to suspect that this footage is AI-altered. Russian forces have increasingly published suspicious footage to propagate claims of expansive Russian advances for informational effects. Order of Battle: Russian sources claimed that elements of the Russian 34th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade (49th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Southern Military District [SMD]) seized Artilne, the first evidence ISW has observed of this brigade in the Velykyi Burluk direction. ISW has recently observed elements of the Russian 34th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade operating in both the Dnipro and Zaporizhia directions. Evidence of the Russian 34th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade operating in the Velyky Burluk direction on July 22 indicates that the Russian military command likely redeployed elements of the brigade to the Velykyi Burluk direction and split the brigade between the Velykyi Burluk axis and the Dnipro and Zaporizhia directions. Geolocated footage published on July 18 shows a Ukrainian MiG-29 Fulcrum striking a Russian drone control point east of Kurylivka with two GBU-39 guided glide bombs. Russian forces are reportedly struggling to advance in the Kupyansk direction reportedly due to Ukrainian forces’ drone density and Russian forces’ shortage of trained personnel and gasoline. A spokesperson for a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Kupyansk direction reported on July 22 that a high density of Ukrainian drone activity in the Kupyansk direction is preventing Russian forces from operating significant amounts of drones, including Lancet and Molniya-type strike drones. The Ukrainian spokesperson reported that elements of Russian 347th Motorized Rifle Regiment (47th Tank Division, 68th Army Corps [AC], Eastern Military District [EMD]) operating in the Kupyansk direction are facing an acute fuel shortage, restricting their use of motorcycles, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), and passenger vehicles. The spokesperson reported that Russian forces are unable to conduct active offensive operations because of a shortage of trained personnel. A Russian milblogger claimed that Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in the Borova direction on July 22, but Russian forces did not advance. Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-range strike campaign against energy infrastructure in occupied Luhansk Oblast. Ukrainian Luhansk Oblast Military Administration Head Oleksiy Kharchenko reported on July 22 that Ukrainian forces struck two power substations in occupied Bila Hora (roughly 10 kilometers from the frontline) and Bezhynove (roughly 80 kilometers from the frontline). A spokesperson for a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Slovyansk direction reported on July 22 that Russian forces are intensifying small infantry group assaults in the Slovyansk direction despite taking high losses. Russian authorities continue costly efforts to mitigate the loss of Russian oil refining capacity due to Ukrainian long-range strikes by subsidizing diesel imports. The Russian State Duma unanimously adopted a bill in its third reading on July 21 that amends the Russian Tax Code and expands the fuel price damping mechanism to diesel exports during active diesel export bans. The bill authorizes the Russian government to compensate Russian oil companies from the federal budget for selling diesel domestically below export prices — a mechanism similar to the one that Russian authorities implemented for imported gasoline on June 23. The July 21 bill increases the compensation coefficient for Belarusian diesel imports to 0.9 and allows vertically-owned Russian oil companies to sell less diesel on the public exchange than otherwise required by law, incentivizing domestic sales. The bill also clarifies the excise tax mechanism for blending gasoline with other components. Russian State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin stated on July 21 that the bill will ensure uninterrupted domestic diesel supplies and claimed that the Russian fuel market will stabilize soon. Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Alexander Novak claimed on July 21 that the Kremlin’s measures to stabilize the fuel market are yielding results as many Russian federal subjects are lifting fuel restrictions, the number of gas stations selling fuel is increasing, and the lines at gas stations are shrinking. Russian officials continue to project a facade of stability and control over domestic fuel supplies despite the fact that Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign has substantially reduced Russia’s oil refining capacity. Toplines The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) appears committed to optimizing Russian forces for continued positional warfare in Ukraine — not for the mechanized maneuver required to make rapid, large-scale gains. Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov held a Russian MoD board meeting on July 17 with deputy defense ministers Alexey Krivoruchko, Dmitry Shcherbinin, Vasily Osmarov, Anna Tsivileva, and Army General Yunus-Bek Yevkurov; Deputy Defense Minister for Logistics Colonel General Alexander Sanchik; First Deputy Defense Minister Leonid Gornin; and Russian State Council Secretary Alexei Dyumin to discuss the progress toward achieving objectives that the board set at the end of 2025. Sanchik and Krivoruchko emphasized that the Russian MoD improved the mobility of Russian assault units by prioritizing the procurement of small, motorized vehicles such as motorcycles, buggies, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Sanchik added that Russia increased supply deliveries on the battlefield by integrating unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Krivoruchko claimed that Russian forces trained 8,000 UAV specialists in the first half of 2026 and that the MoD more than doubled its drone deliveries to Russian troops from 2025 deliveries. ISW has previously assessed that Russian forces are experiencing administrative and training bottlenecks for recruitment of drone operators and continue facing specialists’ shortages in unmanned systems units amid declining recruitment rates, contrary to Krivoruchko’s claims. Sanchik and Krivoruchko’s statements indicate that Russian forces continued to prioritize and optimize for attacks on small, motorized vehicles over armored mechanized vehicles such as tanks and continued supplying kit such as UGVs to sustain forces in “kill zone” and positional warfare conditions. The Russian MoD therefore remained committed to enabling Russian forces to facilitate slow, grinding advances rather than resuming fast-paced maneuver warfare, as senior Russian defense officials previously outlined these optimizations during the last Russian MoD board meeting on December 17, 2025. Russian forces are actively continuing to prioritize a mode of warfare that is failing to enable them to advance. ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces are losing 1.6 square kilometers per day thus far in July 2026 and will likely continue to struggle to achieve meaningful territorial advances as they have in recent months. Russia’s prioritization of its war efforts in Ukraine and suboptimal economic policies are reportedly triggering a broader economic decline in Russia. The Moscow Exchange Composite Stock Index (IMOEX) fell by 4.24 percent to about 2,022 points at the end of the day on July 16 — marking the steepest single-day decline since September 26, 2022 — and declined again to 1,958 points on July 17 by the end of the main trading session. Russian majority state-owned VTB Bank’s shares on the IMOEX Index fell by six percent to an all-time low of 57.8 rubles (about $0.74) per share on July 16. The Russian Central Bank reported July 15 that its Business Climate Indicator (BCI) decreased by 4.5 points to negative 3.6 points in July 2026 — the lowest level since April 2022 and lower than after the Fall 2022 partial mobilization. The BCI is a monthly survey-based measure of economic activity in Russia designed to show how businesses assess their current economic conditions. The Russian economy is likely experiencing a financial decline that extends beyond the recent fuel shortages across Russia and occupied Ukraine amid Ukraine’s strike campaign against Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure. Russia’s emphasis on sustaining the war effort and building up its defense industrial base (DIB) throughout the war has, in part, led to many of Russia’s current economic issues, including increased and unsustainable war spending, growing inflation, significant labor shortages within the construction and services industries, and reductions in Russia’s sovereign wealth fund. Devaluations of Russian state-owned banks, along with Russia’s ongoing and escalating nationalization campaign, likely deter stakeholders from investing in the Russian economy. These factors, including Russia’s censorship campaign to control internet access that impacts Russians’ ability to conduct business, likely also have a compounding negative effect on Russia’s economic performance that the Kremlin will likely fail to adequately address in the mid- to long term. A Russian state-affiliated polling center recorded one of the sharpest drops in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s approval ratings since the start of the war in Ukraine following several months of steady decline. The Kremlin-linked Public Opinion Foundation (FOM) published on July 17 the results of a poll taken from July 10 to 12, measuring a five percent drop in Putin’s approval rating to about 66 percent, one of the largest drops in Putin’s approval rating since February 2022. The FOM also recorded that trust levels in Putin dropped from 69 to 67 percent in the same time period. The FOM’s drop in Putin’s approval ratings now coheres more closely with the polling from the Russian state-owned All-Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VTsIOM), which recorded Putin’s approval rating at about 66 percent in a poll published on July 10. Both the FOM and VTsIOM have recorded relatively steady declines in Putin’s approval and trust ratings since March 2026, but the percentage points that each has published have not closely cohered until now despite both having connections to the Russian government. Data from the FOM and VTsIOM remains unreliable in terms of gauging what percentage of Russians are actually discontent with the Russian government, but it remains notable that Russian state-owned and state-affiliated polling centers believe it necessary to acknowledge growing societal discontent that is likely related to the broader costs of the Russian war effort in Ukraine, which are increasingly burdening ordinary Russians. Former Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD) advisor on defense technology and drone and electronic warfare (EW) expert Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov reported on July 15 that a Russian-guided Shahed drone flew along the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, changed its trajectory above the M-07 Korosten-Kyiv City highway in Korosten, and struck a gas station in Malyn, Zhytomyr Oblast, at a distance of 260 kilometers from the Russian border. Toplines Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) recruitment programs are reportedly failing to compensate for the rising Russian casualty rate amid costly advances in Ukraine. The Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) reported on July 12 that the Russian MoD recruited about 195,000 personnel contract soldiers as of early July 2026 — less than 50 percent of Russia’s annual contract recruitment goal of 409,000. SZRU reported that Russia’s daily recruitment rate fell from about 1,200 people per day in 2024 to 1090 recruits per day in mid-2026 and noted that Russia’s recruitment rate is insufficient to accomplish Russia’s annual goal. SZRU noted that growing battlefield losses have forced the Russian MoD to relax its medical and other administrative standards for recruiting candidates and intensify efforts to recruit students, foreigners, and residents in Russian-occupied Ukraine. Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief General Oleksandr Syrskyi reported on July 14 that Russian forces currently suffer over 400 casualties per each square kilometer that Russian forces seize in Donetsk Oblast. ISW previously assessed that Russian forces suffered around 1,298 casualties per square kilometer they seized or infiltrated in June 2026 compared to an average of 68 casualties per kilometer seized in June 2025 at the theater level. ISW’s calculations differ from those in Syrskyi’s statement due to a number of methodological factors. ISW’s assessment accounts for theater-wide casualties while Syrskyi’s figures specifically refer to the Donetsk Oblast. ISW is unable to independently estimate Russian casualty levels within individual Ukrainian oblasts. It is also unclear how Syrskyi’s statistics account for the areas in which Russian forces conduct infiltration missions, suffer casualties, but do not successfully seize. Ukrainian forces also recently liberated areas near Lyman, and it remains unclear how territorial control changes resulting from newly Ukrainian liberated-territories factor into the Russian casualty rate when calculating the quantity of square kilometers that Russian forces seized. Syrskyi’s figures all the same provide a helpful metric for quantifying the overarching trend in how Russian forces pay very steep prices for meager tactical gains, regardless of the specific methods used to quantify such figures. Russia’s high casualty rates, regardless of calculation method, reflect Ukraine’s ability to undermine Russian battlefield operations and inflict significant personnel losses. Russia’s casualty rate overtook its recruitment rate in March 2026, and Russian forces will likely continue struggling to generate replacements amid the rising casualty rate without compulsory mobilization. The Coalition of the Willing reaffirmed the necessity that Ukraine receive binding security guarantees as part of a larger peace plan and reiterated the members’ commitment to participate in peace negotiations. The Coalition of the Willing met in Paris on July 13 and issued a joint statement reaffirming its support for Ukraine, calling for an “immediate and complete ceasefire” in Ukraine and direct peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with the participation of the United States and Europe. The coalition reiterated that there can be no meaningful peace agreements surrounding Ukrainian and European interests and security without Ukrainian and European participation. The coalition supported US President Donald Trump’s July 7 statement at the NATO Summit in Ankara in support of providing security guarantees to Ukraine. The coalition emphasized that politically and legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine are essential for a durable peace following a ceasefire to deter future Russian aggression and to European stability and security. The Kremlin continues to reject security guarantees for Ukraine and seeks to deny European participation in peace negotiations on Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed on July 14 that unspecified “Europeans” are attempting to undermine unspecified “existing agreements” between Russia and the United States, possibly referencing the supposed agreements that the Kremlin claims the US and Russia reached at the August 2025 Alaska Summit, but that in fact were never reached. Lavrov reiterated Russian President Vladimir Putin‘s June 2024 speech emphasizing Russia‘s maximalist war aims, including Ukraine’s complete withdrawal from Ukrainian-controlled territory in Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts and the abandonment of Ukraine’s NATO accession aspirations before Russia would agree to a ceasefire and start peace negotiations. Lavrov reiterated that US President Donald Trump and Putin “concluded” an agreement during the August 2025 Alaska Summit in Anchorage but acknowledged that the US and Russia did not sign any documents formalizing any agreement. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed on June 25 that Russia and the United States did not reach any agreement to end Russia’s war in Ukraine during the August 2025 Alaska Summit. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on July 14 that Russia opposes European participation in peace negotiations and added that Russia will not agree to any security guarantees for Ukraine without Russia’s participation, rejecting US President Donald Trump’s and the Coalition of the Wiling’s efforts to facilitate a lasting peace in Ukraine. The Kremlin has routinely tried to exclude European leaders from being involved in the peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, including rejecting proposals for European peacekeepers and security guarantees and portraying the United States and Russia as the only relevant negotiating actors. The Kremlin’s repeated rejection of any meaningful Western security guarantees for Ukraine further demonstrates Russia’s unwillingness to accept any agreement that falls short of Ukraine’s full capitulation. Ukraine’s Western partners continue efforts to boost Ukraine’s air defense umbrella, particularly to combat Russian ballistic missiles. Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine signed a joint declaration at the Coalition of the Willing meeting on July 13 in Paris to create the Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition to accelerate the production of anti-ballistic air defense systems. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that he hopes Ukraine’s Freyja anti-ballistic missile interceptor will be in operation within the next 12 months (by mid-July 2027). Zelensky added that Ukraine will be the first to receive the new Franco-Italian Sol-Air Moyenne-Portée/Terrestre New Generation (SAMP/T NG) air defense systems and that France will provide Ukraine with two SAMP/T systems in 2026. Ukrainian forces downed five of the eight ballistic missiles Russian forces launched on the night of July 13 to 14 — a notably higher interception rate compared to the past five Russian strike packages that included ballistic missiles, in which Ukrainian forces downed none of the missiles. Russian forces have been taking advantage of Ukraine’s depleted stocks of Patriot missile interceptors in recent weeks to maximize the destructive potential of their strike packages. European efforts to boost Ukraine’s anti-ballistic air defense umbrella will complement US efforts to grant Ukraine a license to produce an unspecified type of interceptor missile for Patriot air defense systems, which are critical for Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian ballistic missiles. France and Italy granted Ukraine licenses to produce Franco-Italian glide bombs and French SCALP missiles in Ukraine, as Ukraine’s partners continue efforts to boost Ukraine’s own defense industrial base (DIB). Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and French President Emmanuel Macron announced on July 14 that France granted Ukraine the licenses to produce Armement Air-Sol Modulaire (AASM) precision-guided glide bombs and SCALP cruise missiles in Ukraine. France and Italy also granted Ukraine the licenses to produce Aster 30 surface-to-air missiles in Ukraine until the end of 2026. The joint declaration also announced Ukraine’s initial order of 16 French Rafale fighter jets from the total 100 that Ukraine stated it would buy in November 2025. France will transfer the first four Rafale fighter jets after Ukrainian personnel complete training for pilots and mechanics, which could begin in France in 2026. The joint declaration added that France will deliver air-to-ground and air-to-air missiles, including laser-guided anti-drone missiles, Missile d’Interception de Combat et d’Auto-defense (MICA) missiles, and beyond-visual-range air-to-air METEOR missiles. Ukraine’s growing fleet of Rafale jets could enable Ukraine to launch more SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles to augment and sustain its intermediate-range strike campaign. Ukrainian forces struck the Salavat Oil Refinery on the night of July 13 to 14, the only major Russian refinery that Ukrainian forces had not previously struck in 2026. The Ukrainian General Staff and Ukrainian Special Operations Forces (SSO) reported that Ukrainian forces struck the Gazprom Neftokhim Salavat Oil Refinery in Salavat, Republic of Bashkortostan (roughly 1,300 kilometers from the international border), resulting in a fire and damaging the AVT-6 primary oil distillation unit and other production facilities. A Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel reported that satellite imagery collected on July 14 indicates that the Ukrainian strikes struck both the AVT-6 and AVT-4 primary processing units. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that the Salavat refinery is one of the largest in Russia and has a processing capacity of about 10 million tons of oil per year. The Ukrainian SSO reported that the refinery was the last major Russian gasoline production facility that Ukrainian forces had not struck thus far in 2026 and that Ukrainian drones traveled roughly 1,500 kilometers from their launch point to the refinery. Geolocated footage published on July 14 shows fire and smoke coming from the Salavat Oil Refinery. Republic of Bashkortostan Head Radiy Khabirov acknowledged that Ukrainian drones targeted an industrial area in Salavat. Russian officials appear to have been unable to provide sufficient air defense protections for the refinery, despite the established pattern that Ukraine has been targeting major refineries since Spring 2026. The Ukrainian General Staff also reported that Ukrainian forces struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Afipsky, Krasnodar Krai (roughly 375 kilometers from the frontline) and a transshipment area near Gelendzhik, Krasnodar Krai (roughly 370 kilometers from the frontline) overnight. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that the Afipsky Oil Refinery is one of the key oil enterprises in southern Russia with a production capacity of about 6.25 million tons per year. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Russian forces use the transshipment infrastructure near Gelendzhik to ship oil and support Russian military and naval logistics. Imagery published on July 14 reportedly shows a fire at Afipsky Oil Refinery. On July 14, the Krasnodar Krai Operational Headquarters acknowledged a fire at the refinery. Ukraine’s ongoing strike campaign against energy infrastructure in Crimea is affecting the region’s agricultural sector. Crimea-based Telegram channel Crimean Wind claimed that Ukrainian forces struck the Balaklava Thermal Power Plant (TPP) in occupied Sevastopol (about 240 kilometers from the frontline) on the night of July 13 to 14, starting a fire and causing unspecified “serious” damage. Sevastopol occupation head Mikhail Razvozhaev claimed on July 14 that a large-scale Ukrainian strike against energy infrastructure in Sevastopol overnight left part of the city without power and forced authorities to implement a rolling blackout schedule. Chairperson of the Crimean Tatar Mejlis Refat Chubarov stated on July 14 that many enterprises in occupied Crimea, particularly small- and medium-sized businesses and those in the agricultural sector, have stopped work due to electricity outages and fuel shortages. Chubarov reported that many livestock and poultry farms are now manually performing processes that were previously mechanized due to power outages. Chubarov added that prolonged power outages in northern Crimea are also affecting the water supply. The Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) similarly reported on July 10 that farmers in Russia are complaining about fuel supply shortages that will likely lead to a reduced harvest this season.
